extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century philosophical treatment of induction, causation, and the logic of scientific explanation that critiques rival views (Whewell, Spencer, etc.) and articulates standards for legitimate inductive reasoning and causal attribution. The excerpt addresses when inductions are legitimate, how explanations differ from descriptions, and ordinary vs scientific uses of causal language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of necessary and universal truths by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be necessary and universal truths expressible in propositions of axiomatic simplicity and obviousness, experience ought to suggest them most readily, clearly, and unceasingly; such truths verify themselves in every instance and, if simple and intelligible, their verification must be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that universal, necessary truths (when they concern the elements of experience) are continually suggested by observation; their pervasiveness, truth, and simplicity secure implicit assent and make them part of the mental picture of the object. Example language: 'A truth, necessary and universal, relative to any object of our knowledge, must verify itself in every instance... all propositions become not only untrue but inconceivable, if ... axioms be violated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axiom for inductive reasoning (mark principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of reasoning depends on the axiom that 'whatever has a mark, has what it is a mark of' (i.e., that a sign indicates the thing signified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill contends that even if this axiom ultimately rests on the Universal Postulate, any fallibility is incurred at the first step and is not increased by repeating the axiom through a chain of reasoning. This is his reply to Spencer's worry that longer arguments compound risk: the initial use of the axiom is the locus of risk, not each repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of inference vs. sources of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolongation of the inferential process can introduce additional chances of casual error (carelessness, ambiguous terms), but these are not the fundamental source of fallacy; long trains of reasoning are often applied to subjects best fortified against the most dangerous causes of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill acknowledges some increased risk from careless steps in long arguments, but argues that more serious fallacies arise from ambiguity and conceptual confusion rather than sheer length. Example: mathematics has very long trains yet is well-fortified against such errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between conception and belief ('I am' formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding 'I am' to a conception marks the transition from mere conception to belief; the phrase 'to conceive that I am' or 'that anything is' departs from rigorous use of the term conceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill uses this linguistic distinction to analyze psychological states relevant to epistemology: conceiving a scene vs believing it to obtain here and now. This criterion helps evaluate claims about subjective apprehension versus asserted belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of practical (non-scientific) inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences drawn in practical life—directly from known cases to a case supposed to be similar—are legitimate and substantially the same operation as scientific induction, even when they lack an expressed general proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to Whewell, Mill argues that restricting 'induction' to only consciously generalized scientific cases is arbitrary. Everyday reasoning (including that of animals or unreflective humans) can be induction without explicit general formulation; the difference is that science records general laws while practical inference is for instantaneous use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions vs. Inductions vs. Explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions are modes of representing facts (how things appear or 'as if' accounts) while explanations attempt to ascribe mechanisms or causes; the same description can be consistent with multiple explanations, but explanations that posit conflicting mechanisms may be mutually exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill illustrates with historical examples (vortices vs Newtonian inverse-square force): as mere descriptions these theories might coincide in results, but as explanations that posit different agents/mechanisms they can contradict and cannot both be true. Use this distinction when evaluating whether two accounts truly conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatibility of contradictory explanations and predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different explanations of the same fact cannot both be true if they assert incompatible mechanisms; similarly, conflicting empirical predictions (e.g., different return periods for a comet) cannot both be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes that when explanations imply different causal laws or yield contradictory predictions, they are logically incompatible. Examples: vortices vs Newtonian gravity; competing predictions about comet returns or voyages of exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope requirement for the uniformity of nature in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition of valid induction is uniformity in the course of nature, but it need only pervade the particular class of phenomena to which the induction relates, not necessarily all phenomena universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill points out that induction about planetary motions or magnetism would stand even if meteorological phenomena were irregular, provided regular laws govern the class considered. The practical inference requires either that uniformity be already known for that class or that we are now entitled to conclude it from evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative criterion for assigning causes in ordinary language
rubrics_metrics.description: In common discourse we often call as 'the cause' the antecedent condition which it is useful or necessary to mention to the hearer — not strictly only the element exerting active force; proximate vs remote causes and positive vs negative conditions are named according to informativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill explains that calling something the cause is frequently governed by whether stating it supplies the information sought (e.g., saying someone died 'because he could not swim' emphasizes the informative negative condition). He gives examples (bribe vs sentinel absent; body possession as necessary condition of death) to show how ordinary causal attributions are pragmatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative conditions and the formula of absence of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula that includes all negative conditions of an effect in the single condition 'absence of counteracting causes' is generally applicable; apparent exceptions (e.g., opacity as a purely preventive property) do not vitiate the practical use of the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill admits some properties seem purely preventive (opacity intercepting light) but suggests these may be explainable in terms of other relations; the practical causal formula remains serviceable even if some counteracting agencies act only by prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of causation to human will (compatibilist standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinations of human will can be regarded as following from motives by law-like regularity: to say actions necessarily follow from character means they invariably do so and would be predictable by someone who completely knew the character; this need not conflict with consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill reserves fuller treatment for later but here defends the view that human actions can be subject to causal regularities analogous to physical causes (compatibilist stance). He cautions that objections often rest on a confusion over the ordinary sense of 'necessity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about hypothetical assumptions in theoretical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theoretical suppositions (e.g., assumed molecular motion in combustible processes) are highly hypothetical and should be recognized as such rather than treated as certain facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill warns that attributing detailed unseen processes (like molecular motion equivalent to combustion energy) may be unnecessary and extravagantly hypothetical; theoretical claims should be distinguished from securely established inductions.
